Q1. Which of the following statements is correct?
A. We can treat a cyclist as a perfect sphere when analyzing the detailed motion
of the cyclist’s ankle.
This is a poor approximation because ankle motion depends on the cyclist’s shape and joint
geometry, which a sphere cannot capture.
B. We can safely model a delivery truck as a point mass when studying how far
it travels over several kilometers.
Over kilometer-scale position changes, the truck’s size is negligible compared with the distance
traveled, so a point-mass model is appropriate.
C. We must never assume motion occurs in a vacuum, even when we intentionally
neglect drag forces.
Neglecting air resistance is often modeled by assuming vacuum-like conditions, so this “never”
claim is too strong.
D. None of the above is correct.
Option B is correct, so “none of the above” cannot be correct.

Q2. Which of the following equations is correct?
A. 1 cm = 1 m.
This ignores the scale factor between centimeters and meters (1 m = 100 cm).
B. 1 = 0.01.
This confuses a conversion factor with an equality between dimensionless numbers.
C. 1 cm = 0.01 m.
Since 100 cm = 1 m, dividing by 100 gives 1 cm = 0.01 m.
D. 100 cm = 0.01 m.
This inverts the conversion because 100 cm equals 1 m, not 0.01 m.

A. Pressure: pascal
Pascal (N/m2
) is the correct SI unit for pressure.
B. Momentum: kg · m/s
kg · m/s is the correct unit for linear momentum.
C. Power: joule
Power is energy per time, so its SI unit is watt (J/s), not joule.

Coulomb is the correct SI unit for electric charge.

Q7. A soccer ball is kicked with a speed v0 at an angle θ above the horizontal.
What is the speed of the ball when it is at the maximum height? (Neglect air
resistance.)
A. v0.
The speed is not generally the launch speed because the vertical component decreases to zero
at the top.
B. v0 cos θ.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component remains v0 cos θ,
so the speed equals v0 cos θ.
C. v0 sin θ.
This is the initial vertical component, but at maximum height the vertical component is zero.
D. 0.
Only the vertical component becomes zero at the top; the horizontal component generally
remains nonzero.

Q9. If the magnitudes of both charges are doubled and their separation is in￾creased by a factor of 4, what happens to the magnitude of the electrostatic force
that each charge exerts on the other?
A. It stays the same.
This ignores that Coulomb’s law scales as q1q2/r2
, so changing both q and r generally changes
the force.
B. It decreases by a factor of 4.
Since F ∝ q1q2/r2
, doubling both charges gives a factor of 4 while increasing distance by 4 gives
a factor of 16 in the denominator, so F becomes 4/16 = 1/4 of the original.
C. It increases by a factor of 4.
This accounts for doubling charges but forgets that increasing separation reduces force by the
square of the distance factor.
D. It increases by a factor of 16.
This incorrectly treats the distance change as increasing the force rather than decreasing it via
r
2
.
E. It decreases by a factor of 2.
This is a common arithmetic slip that does not correctly combine the ×4 charge effect with the
÷16 distance-squared effect.

Q11. The force F⃗ = (−2.50 N)ˆı + (6.00 N)ˆȷ acts on a particle as it moves along
the y axis from y = 1.20 m to y = 4.70 m. What is the work, in joules, done by
the force on the particle?
A. 21.0 J.
The displacement is ∆⃗r = (3.50 m)ˆȷ, so W = F⃗ · ∆⃗r = (6.00)(3.50) = 21.0 J.
B. −8.75 J.
This incorrectly uses the x-component of force even though the displacement is purely along y.
C. 8.75 J.
This takes the magnitude of the x-component contribution, but there is no x-displacement so
the x-force does no work.
D. 27.5 J.
This commonly comes from using the force magnitude times distance instead of the dot product
with the correct direction.

Q12. A 3.0 kg cart initially moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a bumper and
rebounds at a speed of 1.5 m/s moving backward. The collision lasts for 0.25 s.
What is the average force exerted on the cart during the collision?
A. 66 N.
Taking the initial direction as positive, ∆p = m(vf − vi) = 3.0(−1.5 − 4.0) = −16.5 N · s, so
|Favg| = |∆p|/∆t = 16.5/0.25 = 66 N.
B. 16.5 N.
This forgets to divide the impulse by the collision time to get average force.
C. 132 N.
This typically comes from doubling the correct force by mishandling the sign change or using
the wrong time interval.
D. None of the above is correct.
Option A is correct because it correctly applies impulse-momentum over the given time.

is caught and held in the glove (the ball and catcher move together immediately
after the catch). What is the speed of the catcher after catching the ball?
A. 0.069 m/s.
Using momentum conservation, v =

85+0.145 ≈ 0.069 m/s.
B. 0.83 m/s.
This typically results from forgetting to divide by the catcher’s mass (treating mbvb as a speed).
C. 40 m/s.
